text: The Azure integration runtime is genuinely fully managed — but it lives inside Azure's own network, with no way to reach a SQL Server sitting behind your corporate firewall. The self-hosted integration runtime closes exactly that gap: real software, the Microsoft Integration Runtime Configuration Manager, that you install yourself on a machine inside the network where your data actually lives.

From Manage, Integration runtimes, New, you get three real choices. Azure runs fully managed compute in Azure. Self-hosted installs on a machine you control. And Linked Self-Hosted reuses a self-hosted IR that already exists in a different data factory or Synapse workspace, so you're not standing up duplicate infrastructure.

Naming a self-hosted IR generates two real authentication keys, a primary and a secondary, so you can rotate one without downtime. Install the Configuration Manager on the target machine, paste in a key, and it registers itself directly against your data factory — a green checkmark confirms the node is live and available.

A self-hosted IR genuinely isn't one machine — it's a logical runtime that can be backed by up to four physical nodes, all sharing the same authentication key. Multiple nodes buy you real high availability, since the others keep serving if one goes down, and real scalability, since more nodes means more concurrent data-movement throughput. Microsoft recommends at least two nodes for any production setup.

Notice the self-hosted IR always initiates its own outbound connection to Azure — nobody has to open an inbound port into your network for any of this to work. Next: Connecting to On-Premises Data Securely, the exact firewall rules a real network admin needs to approve.
